text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright said on Monday that comparisons between Germany's contemporary handling of Scientologists and Nazi extermination of Jews were inccurate and distasteful.

Wrapping up the second stop on her tour of nine world capitals, Albright went out of her way to play down U.S. differences with Bonn on Scientology and to accentuate harmony on plans to expand NATO and persuade Russia to accept the alliance bringing former communist states into its fold.

But German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel said Bonn still remained interested in a French proposal for a five-nation mini-summit on NATO expansion with Russia, despite oppposition from the United States and smaller alliance members like Italy.
Differences also persisted in approaches to "rogue" states and there was a long discussion between Albright and Kinkel on this issue, especially Iran, but also Iraq nd Libya, U.S. officials said.

The State Department in its annual human reports recently accused Germany of harassing Scientologists, whose members in the United States include many prominent entertainers, such as Tom Cruise and Chick Corea.

But Albright stressed that differences over this subject could be handled amicably on a bilateral basis and she strongly attacked Scientologsts for accusing Germany of acting toward them as Nazis had treated Jews.

"Clearly it's a subject that needs to be worked out in bilateral relations. But I must say that any discussion which draws comparisans between what happened under the Nazis and what is happening now is historically inaccurate and totally distasteful," she told a joint news conference with Kinkel.

U.S. officials said Kinkel raised the issue and it was discussed for about two minutes at the end of the ministers' one hour meeting. Albright, making her first visit to Europe and Asia since becoming secretary of state, also spent 75 minutes with Chancellor Helmut Kohl.

Kinkel told reporters Scientologists were not persecuted in Germany and he stressed that under German law, Scientology was considered a profit-making organisation rather than a religion. In the United States, by comparison, Scientology was considered a religion and therefore tax exempt.
But he insisted this is "not an issue that plays a decisive part in (U.S.-German) bilateral relations" and urged that "we should play it down."

A major focus of Albright's trip to Europe is to consolidate the alliance position on NATO expansion and the package of inducements and assurances being offered to persuade Moscow to accept expansion and sign a charter defining a special relationship between NATO and Russia.
Kinkel travels to Moscow to discuss NATO with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov and Albright visits the Russian capital several days later.

The alliance plans a summit in Madrid in July to decide on new NATO members but France has proposed a mini-summit to precede that involving the four major NATO members -- the United States, Frace, Germany and Britain -- plus Russia.
Albright contnued to rule that out, saying the alliance was now focused on the substance of Madrid not process.
But Kinkel indicated continued openness to the mini-summit idea, saying: "We have to do everything we can to make it easier for the Russian people to accept NATO enlargement."

On Iran, U.S. officials said German leaders indicated growing hand-wringing over the European policy of maintaining a critical dialogue with Teheran, which Washington accuses of spnsoring state terrorism.

A German court is due to rule on a 1991 case in which a Berlin restaurant was bombed killing four Iranian opposition leaders. German leaders are worried that if Iran was found to be behind the bombing it could increase domestic pressure to cut ties with and punish Iran, as the United States has done.
Albright later flies to Paris and is also due to visit Brussels, London, Moscow, Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing.
